fieldData.description:
Built for speed in a changing world

Coelophysis was one of the earliest successful theropod dinosaurs, living during the Late Triassic around 210 million years ago. Unlike the massive predators that would dominate later in the Jurassic and Cretaceous, Coelophysis was lightweight, slender and highly agile. Its long legs, narrow body and balancing tail made it an efficient runner capable of quickly chasing prey across dry floodplains and open woodlands.

Its skeleton reveals many features that would later define theropod dinosaurs. Hollow bones reduced body weight, while sharp teeth and grasping hands made it a capable predator. Although relatively small, Coelophysis was likely an active hunter that fed on lizards, small reptiles and other early vertebrates. Some scientists also believe it may have scavenged opportunistically when food was scarce.

One of the reasons Coelophysis became so famous is the enormous fossil site discovered at Ghost Ranch in New Mexico. Hundreds of skeletons were found together, preserved in ancient river sediments. This mass accumulation may have formed after seasonal droughts and sudden flooding events, offering an extraordinary glimpse into Triassic ecosystems.

Coelophysis lived during a time of major evolutionary change. Dinosaurs were only beginning to rise to dominance, sharing the world with crocodile relatives, amphibians and many strange reptilian species that would later disappear. Its success demonstrates how early theropods were already developing the speed, balance and predatory adaptations that would eventually lead to iconic dinosaurs like Allosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.

Today, Coelophysis remains one of the most important dinosaurs for understanding the origins of theropods and the early evolution of dinosaurs as a whole.
fieldData.typical-features:
• Lightweight, hollow bones built for speed
  • Long, slender legs adapted for fast running
  • Narrow skull filled with sharp, serrated teeth
  • Long tail used for balance while moving
  • Three-fingered hands capable of grasping prey
  • Slim, agile body compared to later large theropods
  • Large eye sockets suggesting strong vision
  • One of the earliest recognizable theropod body plans
  • Flexible neck for quick strikes and scanning surroundings
  • Small but efficient predator adapted to harsh Triassic environments
fieldData.name: Coelophysis

fieldData.description:
The armored giant of the Jurassic

Stegosaurus was one of the most iconic herbivorous dinosaurs of the Late Jurassic. Instantly recognizable by the large plates along its back and the deadly spikes at the end of its tail, it roamed the floodplains of what is now North America around 155 million years ago.

Although massive in size, Stegosaurus was a relatively slow-moving plant eater that fed mainly on low vegetation such as ferns, cycads, horsetails, and shrubs. Its long hind legs and shorter front legs gave it a distinctive sloping posture, while its narrow beaked mouth was adapted for cropping soft plants rather than chewing tough vegetation.

Its famous back plates are still debated by scientists today. They may have been used for display, species recognition, temperature regulation, or attracting mates. The tail spikes, however, clearly served as powerful defensive weapons against predators such as Allosaurus.

Stegosaurus lived in a rich Jurassic ecosystem alongside giant sauropods, early mammals, crocodilians, and some of the most famous carnivorous dinosaurs in prehistoric history.
fieldData.typical-features:
• Large double row of back plates
  • Four long tail spikes (“thagomizer”)
  • Small head with a beak-like mouth
  • Powerful hind legs and shorter front legs
  • Low-slung posture
  • Tiny brain relative to body size
  • Heavily armored appearance
fieldData.name: Stegosaurus

fieldData.description:
The Last Giant of the Cretaceous

Few dinosaurs are as instantly recognizable as Triceratops. With its three formidable horns, massive bony frill, and rhinoceros-like build, it became one of the defining icons of prehistoric life — a symbol of the final age of dinosaurs before the end-Cretaceous extinction reshaped life on Earth.

Triceratops roamed the lush floodplains and forests of western North America approximately 68 to 66 million years ago, during the closing chapter of the Late Cretaceous. It lived in a world filled with towering conifers, dense vegetation, and some of the most legendary creatures ever discovered, including the fearsome Tyrannosaurus rex.

Despite its intimidating appearance, Triceratops was a herbivore. Its powerful beak and specialized teeth allowed it to slice through tough prehistoric plants with remarkable efficiency. The enormous frill and long facial horns may have served multiple purposes — from defense against predators to display, recognition, and combat between rivals of the same species.

What truly makes Triceratops fascinating is the balance between strength and mystery. Scientists continue to debate how it behaved, how social it may have been, and how exactly it used its iconic horns. Even after more than a century of research, this prehistoric giant still holds secrets beneath the stone.

As one of the last non-avian dinosaurs to walk the Earth, Triceratops represents the dramatic final moments of the dinosaur era — powerful, ancient, and unforgettable.
fieldData.typical-features:
• Three facial horns
  • Large defensive neck frill
  • Powerful parrot-like beak
  • Quadrupedal stance
  • Robust skull structure
fieldData.name: Triceratops
